meta.title: Who really said "Cool Papa was so fast that he could turn off the light switch and get into bed before the room got dark"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Satchel Paige really did tell this one about Cool Papa Bell — but the polished wording is not what any source prints, and the joke was in print by 1917.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Cool Papa was so fast that he could turn off the light switch and get into bed before the room got dark'?
meta.ogDescription: Paige told it about Cool Papa Bell, twice on the record. The joke, though, is fifty years older than he is on it.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1906–1982 · Negro leagues and Major League pitcher
answer.sourceLine: Paige told this one about James “Cool Papa” Bell, and he told it more than once. Quote Investigator ↗ documents him using it in The Washington Post in April 1969 and again in Jet in July 1971. Neither account prints the smooth sentence that circulates today, and the gag was already half a century old when Paige got to it — so we record this as attributed, not verified.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: In print by April 1917, author unknown

source.excerpt: Paige claims to be the best pitcher of all time, although not necessarily the fastest. That distinction, he says, belongs to Cool Papa Bell. “Cool Papa was so fast he could get in bed before the room got dark.”
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ traces the joke to April 1917, in The Marines Magazine, where a Fort Mifflin correspondent writing as “Hablarias” said a fast corporal “can switch off the lights and be back in bed before the room gets dark!”

The same page documents Paige applying it to Bell twice — The Washington Post, 29 April 1969, and Jet, 22 July 1971 — and records the joke passing through vaudeville, a Paul Bunyan story and an Abbott and Costello script in between.

Wikiquote ↗ carries this exact wording and pins it to that same 1969 Washington Post column. Quote Investigator, transcribing the same column, prints a shorter sentence. We could not read the original — it sits behind ProQuest — so we do not assert which of the two is right.

Wikipedia’s article on Bell ↗ gives the story underneath the gag: a hotel where faulty wiring delayed the light going out after the switch was flipped, long enough for Bell to get into bed. Paige, it says, liked to tell it without the explanation.
source.excerptNote: That is the whole of it as The Washington Post of 29 April 1969 is transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗, which adds that “apparently, the reporter or the editor truncated the full description.” Two years later Jet rendered it as “he could turn the light out and be in bed before the room got dark.” Neither is the sentence above.

sourceLink.text: Quote Investigator on the light-switch joke

source.rightsNote: We assert no rights status, because we cannot say where this exact wording was first published. The joke’s earliest documented appearance — The Marines Magazine, April 1917 — is old enough to be in the United States public domain, but it is not this sentence. The two documented Paige versions ran in The Washington Post (1969) and Jet (1971), both far too recent for the public domain, and neither matches the wording above.

author.name: Satchel Paige
author.heading: About Satchel Paige
author.metaLine: 1906–1982 · Negro leagues and Major League pitcher
author.bio: Leroy Robert “Satchel” Paige began pitching in the Negro leagues with the Birmingham Black Barons in 1927 and did not reach the Major Leagues until 9 July 1948, when he debuted for the Cleveland Indians at 42. That season he became the first player who had played in the Negro leagues to pitch in a World Series. He threw his last Major League game for the Kansas City Athletics in September 1965, two weeks shy of 60, and in 1971 became the first player elected by the Hall of Fame’s Negro League Committee.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: Nobody is falsely credited here: Paige really did say it, about Bell, more than once. Two quieter errors travel with the line — the wording has been smoothed, and the joke is not his.

items.why: Writing as “Hablarias” in The Marines Magazine, a correspondent at Fort Mifflin, Pennsylvania said of a fast corporal: “It is 20 feet from the switchboard to his pile of alfalfa and he can switch off the lights and be back in bed before the room gets dark!” Quote Investigator ↗
The Chicago Tribune of 9 March 1919 reported the comedy team using it: “when I go to bed at night and turn out the light I’m in bed before the room is dark.”
A published script with a 1945 copyright has Costello boasting he can “turn off the lights and dive into bed before the room gets dark!” — followed by a loud crash.
Ali was using a first-person version by 1974, and the New York Times printed one in 1975. It is the same gag, reassigned from Bell to himself.

items.who: “turn off the light switch and get into bed”
items.why: This polished form matches neither documented Paige account. The 1969 column is shorter; the 1971 Jet version reads “turn the light out and be in bed.”

misattribution.truthLine: Paige told the joke about Cool Papa Bell and did more than anyone to make it famous — but he was passing on a gag already in print in 1917, and the polished sentence above is not what either documented account of him telling it actually says. Quote Investigator ↗

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: James “Cool Papa” Bell played in the Negro leagues and the Mexican League from 1922 to 1946 and is considered one of the fastest men ever to play the game ↗. He and Paige were Pittsburgh Crawfords teammates in the mid-1930s, and he was elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1974.

The Negro leagues kept thin statistical records, so the case for Bell’s speed was made in stories rather than numbers — and Paige was the best storyteller in the game. Wikipedia records the literal version: a hotel where faulty wiring left a beat between the switch and the dark, enough for Bell to get under the covers. Paige dropped the wiring and kept the miracle.
detailsBody: Quote Investigator’s chronology runs: The Marines Magazine (April 1917); the vaudeville team Moran and Mack in the Chicago Tribune (1919); an Atchison, Kansas wife on her husband and the gas light (1920); Paul Bunyan blowing out a candle (1937); a Washington Post brainteaser (1943); an Abbott and Costello script (1945); Paige on Bell (1969 and 1971); a Washington Post columnist reassigning it to the Padres’ Enzo Hernandez (1973); and Muhammad Ali (1974 and 1975).

That Paige sits two-thirds of the way down a list like this is not a knock on him. The joke survived sixty years because it kept finding people fast enough to carry it, and Bell is the one it stuck to.

schema.verdictNote: Satchel Paige really did say this about Cool Papa Bell: Quote Investigator documents him using the line in The Washington Post (29 April 1969) and in Jet (22 July 1971). What is unconfirmed is this exact wording, which matches neither account, and the joke itself was in print by 1917.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator dates the light-switch joke to April 1917 in The Marines Magazine, and documents Paige using it about Cool Papa Bell in The Washington Post (29 April 1969) and Jet (22 July 1971), noting the 1969 account appears truncated.
Wikiquote carries this exact wording and cites it to The Washington Post, 29 April 1969, p. D2.
Wikipedia records the hotel-wiring story behind the joke, gives Bell’s dates as 1903–1991 and his Hall of Fame election as 1974, and lists him with the Pittsburgh Crawfords 1933–1937.

Wikipedia gives Paige’s dates as July 7, 1906 – June 8, 1982, his Major League debut as July 9, 1948 for the Cleveland Indians, his final game in September 1965 two weeks shy of 60, and his 1971 election as the first Negro League Committee inductee.
